intro: Two boxers in the same weight class fight with padded gloves inside a roped ring, scoring with clean punches to the front and sides of the head and body above the belt. Bouts are divided into timed rounds and won by knockout, stoppage or judges' decision. Olympic-style boxing is governed internationally by World Boxing, while professional boxing is regulated by national and state commissions, with titles sanctioned by several organisations.
inThirtySeconds: Punch only with the knuckle part of a closed glove, above the belt.
Knocked down? The referee counts — still down at 10 is a knockout.
If nobody is stopped, judges score each round, usually 10–9 to the winner.
objective: Win by knockout, by the referee stopping the contest, or on the judges' scorecards.

facts.duration: Olympic-style: 3 × 3 min · Professional: up to 12 × 3 min

scoring.label: 10-point must
scoring.detail: Each judge gives 10 to the round winner and fewer to the loser.

scoring.label: Knockdown
scoring.detail: A knockdown usually costs the fallen boxer an extra point on the cards.

scoring.label: KO / TKO
scoring.detail: Ends the bout immediately, regardless of scorecards.

variants.name: Olympic-style
variants.description: Amateur boxing as contested at the Olympics and World Boxing events: three 3-minute rounds and five judges.

variants.name: Professional
variants.description: Paid boxing regulated by commissions: 4 to 12 rounds, usually three judges, and title belts from sanctioning bodies.

chapters.title: Legal punches
chapters.summary: What counts and where you may hit.

rules.title: The target area
rules.summary: Punches must land with the knuckle part of a closed glove on the front or sides of the head and body, above the belt.
rules.body: The back of the head, the back, the kidneys and anywhere below the belt are illegal targets. Judges reward clean, effective punches, defence, ring generalship and aggression that lands.

rules.title: Holding and clinching
rules.summary: Boxers may not hold, hook an arm or wrestle; the referee separates clinches with 'break'.
rules.body: Repeated holding to avoid punches leads to warnings and point deductions. After 'break' both boxers must step back before punching again.

chapters.title: Knockdowns and stoppages
chapters.summary: The count, the knockout and the referee's role.

rules.title: The count
rules.summary: When a boxer is knocked down, the referee counts to 10; if the boxer can't continue by then, it is a knockout.
rules.body: A boxer is 'down' if any part of the body other than the feet touches the floor, or if they are hanging helplessly on the ropes. The opponent goes to a neutral corner. In many rule sets the count continues to at least eight even if the boxer rises immediately (a mandatory eight count).
rules.example: A fighter is dropped, gets up at the count of six but cannot raise her guard: the referee may stop the bout — a TKO.

rules.title: Referee stops contest (TKO)
rules.summary: The referee, the ringside doctor or a boxer's corner can stop a bout to protect a boxer who cannot defend themselves.
rules.body: This is recorded as a technical knockout (TKO) or 'referee stops contest' (RSC). Cuts judged too dangerous by the doctor can also end a fight.

chapters.title: Judging
chapters.summary: How bouts that go the distance are decided.

rules.title: The 10-point must system
rules.summary: Judges score each round independently, giving 10 points to the winner and 9 or fewer to the loser.
rules.body: At the end, the scores are totalled. A decision can be unanimous (all judges agree), split (judges disagree) or majority (one judge scores a draw). A draw is also possible.

rules.title: Five judges
rules.summary: Olympic-style bouts are scored by five judges over three rounds.
rules.body: The winner is the boxer favoured by the majority of judges. Rules on headguards vary by age group and gender, so check World Boxing's current regulations.

rules.title: Championship rounds
rules.summary: Professional title fights are scheduled for 12 rounds; non-title bouts may be 4, 6, 8 or 10.
rules.body: Professional rules are set by the commission overseeing the event, so details such as the three-knockdown rule or standing eight counts vary between jurisdictions.

fouls.name: Rabbit punch
fouls.description: Hitting the back of the head or neck.

fouls.name: Headbutt
fouls.description: Using the head as a weapon, accidental or deliberate.

fouls.name: Hitting after the bell
fouls.description: Punching once the round has ended or after 'break'.

flow.title: Weigh-in
flow.description: Boxers must make the weight limit of their division.

flow.title: Rounds
flow.description: Three-minute rounds separated by one-minute rests in the corner.

flow.title: Knockdowns
flow.description: Counts and possible stoppages during the bout.

flow.title: Decision
flow.description: If the bout goes the distance, the scorecards are read.

positions.name: Orthodox boxer
positions.role: Leads with the left hand and foot.

positions.name: Southpaw
positions.role: Leads with the right — awkward for orthodox opponents.

positions.name: Corner team
positions.role: Coaches and cutman who advise and treat the boxer between rounds.

field.name: Ring
field.dimensions: Usually between about 4.9 m and 7.3 m square inside the ropes
field.surface: Padded canvas floor surrounded by four ropes
notes: Two corners for the boxers, two neutral corners
The bell signals the start and end of each round

glossary.definition: A quick straight punch with the lead hand.
A straight punch with the rear hand.
A curved punch thrown from the side.
A rising punch aimed at the chin or body.
Technical knockout — the bout is stopped for the boxer's safety.

funFacts: Modern boxing is based on the Marquess of Queensberry Rules of 1867, which introduced gloves and 3-minute rounds.
Boxing has featured at every modern Summer Olympics since 1904 except 1912.
